Author: @vitabricksnailslime8273
Content: Just when you think it's all worked out, there's more to consider. In recent years, a few Aussie Rules footballers have made their way in the NFL due to their kicking proficiency. The Rules football is of a similar size to the American one, but without the acute point. Now in Rules, the longest kicks are obtained by what is called the spiral torpedo. But at the top level, you might be waiting years before you ever saw one. This is because it's really hard to obtain accuracy while imparting spin in the longitudinal axis off the boot. What you will see is the drop punt, where the ball is struck just below the tip, on the chin if you will, to impart end over end spin. These kicks are very accurate and are easy to catch. Goal scoring from outside 50 metres are very common, with the kicker having to back off from where the mark was taken, since a defender will be standing on that spot, and also having to clear the fingertips of rather tall athletes jumping for all they're worth in the goal square. Author: @FoxSterling
Content: Slight error in the mention of arrows. Arrows don't use the fletching as a "parachute" to keep arrowhead forward, the fletching is used to impart a spin. It uses the same spin physics you are talking about a football using. An unspinning arrow will wobble in unpredictable directions. The spin is what keeps the arrow straight, and following it's parabolic arc. When fletching with real feathers, the feathers have to come from the same wing. If you mixed left and right wing feathers on the same arrow, their natural foil would create counter spin, so you'd end up with an unspinning arrow which would not go where you aimed.

Content: The grip stitching on the side of the ball also plays a part in not just its handling and launching, but also its spin. It doesn't weigh very much by comparison to the rest of the ball, but the slight offset of its weight is multiplied once rotation forces begin acting upon it which allows it to maintain a higher degree of stabilizing centrifugal force. It is also why the ball cannot be thrown without even the slightest rotation - no matter how little you manage to influence its rotation, the air will still catch those grooves in the thick white stitching and kick off rotation independent of the passer.

Content: Intuitively, it would seem that the football turns over because the angular momentum keeps the point of the ball aimed in the direction of travel (minimizing wind resistance) while the direction of travel is determined by gravity acting on the ball. If the ball doesn’t turn over, the broad side would be exposed to the direction of travel, which would obviously be suboptimal. I also feel like I’ve thrown spirals that do not wobble (or wobble imperceptibly), both fade passes (high arcing) and frozen ropes. Is there a rate, or rates, of rotation where the wobble stabilizes, possibly dependent on the shape of the parabola or the ball’s velocity? My conjecture would be bullet passes require a higher spin rate to minimize wobble while touch passes would require less.

Author: @NS1718-l9c
Content:
Amazing work with Tom.  Done similar work with Aussie Rules football, largely empirical, combined with engineering and background as a pilot.  It's very well explained by Bernoulli and the Total Pressure = Dynamic + Static Pressure formula.  Total must always be the same across the ball, dynamic changes according to the disposition of the football through the airstream.  Slight tilt up or down, left or right creates changes to dynamic pressures leading to a corresponding balancing of the static pressure.  It's this static pressure differential that results in the movement of the ball in a particular direction.  Same as an airplane wing.  The ball turns over as the dynamic pressure on the bottom of the ball is higher than the top, the static pressure is therefore lower on the bottom which drives movement from the higher static pressure above the ball towards the bottom (static pressure has a tendency to move a body from high pressure area towards the low).

What would have been interesting to see is Tom throwing the football in a variety of wind directions.  My tip is he would have paradoxically got the best distance outcome throwing into a slight headwind - same reason an airplane takes off into wind.  Into wind, the useful pressure dynamic that produces lift (and distance) is present whilst the ball is at rest before he even moves his arm. If the ball had an airspeed indicator attached, it would have an airspeed before it even starts to move across the ground.

Content: 3:45 This is exactly why a knuckleball moves so bizarre. Because the wind picks up one side of the pitch, but then another 2 mph gust hits other side that moves it, so forth and so on across 60.5 ft. Fastballs have spin rates way too fast for wind to just effect one specific square area of a baseball. It spins so much that it will uniformly across all square inches of the surface area of the baseball feel same exact mph wind gust hitting each thread on the baseball. So it then has a linear path to home plate. Knuckleballs go insane on days when the wind is erratically blowing directions.

Author: @av8ing
Content:
As a commercial helicopter pilot and instructor I have heard the term gyroscopic precession used and misunderstood nearly as many times as I have heard it mentioned. This is just as misleading as the FAA and the majority of helicopter pilots saying “hovering auto” when referring to an inertia landing while hovering over a stationary point while in ground effect…..but I digress.  For years the FAA has also incorrectly stated this misleading statement about gyroscopic precession. Finally they have amended the definition to be slightly more accurate. To state that it reaches peak 90° further along from where the force is applied or is felt 90° later in the plane of rotation (paraphrased) is only correct for a given mass at a given RPM. If you change the mass or RPM then the statement is no longer true. If the rpm increases beyond the ideal for a given mass, gyroscopic precession will be advanced and take place beyond 90° in the plane of rotation. Conversely, if the rpm is slowed beyond the ideal point for the given mass the action will be retarded causing the action to be seen closer to the point of input than 90°. And of course this is also only true if conducted in the same or relatively similar gravitational field.

Author: @timapple6586
Content:
Right-hander's ball drifts right, left-hander's ball drifts left. It's simply the Magnus Effect.... altho' I'm sure there are a bajillion 12yr old would-be FPS snipers out there saying it's the Coriolis Effect. Notice that the experimenters in this vid never changed ends or threw cross-field in the other direction. Bad science. And regarding Rice and other receivers, they're locking on their QB's eyes - NOT the ball trajectory. Bad, baaad science. And no, Derek, that is NOT a newtonian "parabolic trajectory" unless you're performing it in a vacuum. You toss up a bomb at a 30º angle and it 'drops' into the receiver's hands 50yds downfield sometimes at a 90º angle like a teardrop-shaped arc. Ballistics. Good math is not a popularity contest. The wobble-theory was mind-bogglingly stupid; the 'turn-over point' is governed entirely by changing where your index finger applies pressure with respect to the ball's center-of-gravity upon release. This is why a good kicker can loop a punt but a QB can't pass around a defender without throwing a 'floater'.
Just put a band-aid or 2 on Tom's right index finger and we'll see how that works out for him. Add all the stickum you want.

Author: @Rocotaco
Content:
10:15
Bullets follow an arch as well, albeit a much smaller arch. Bullets don't just go in a straight line our of the barrel. They start going up slightly as soon as they leave the barrel. I have a rifle that is sighted in at 50 yards. It hits dead center at 50 yards. Putting the crosshairs dead center at 100 yards, this same gun hits HIGHER than at 50 yards because the bullet is still on an upwards trajectory in it's ballistic path. At 200 yards, it hits dead center again as it has started on a downward trajectory. Heavier bullets with lighter powder loads follow this same exact path. If you ever see old WWII rifles (like Mosin Nagants) they have a rear sight with meter distance adjustments. 1000 meters puts the sight far higher because you are essentially doing volley fire due to the distance. The spin can help prevent wind from impacting the ball but it will not prevent the weight of the ball plus the eventual (slow) loss of momentum from causing it to follow an arched trajectory.

Author: @StrugglebusAdv
Content:
So, how does this apply to artillery and bullets, that also follow a ballistic trajectory, but with arguably far less wobble? 

I would expect the gyroscopic spin to keep the axis pointed in the direction of travel. Initially on firing (bullet/artillery shell) or throwing (football), the forces are enough to overcome gravity, thus the direction of travel is up. As it loses upward momentum near the top, it becomes "weightless" or "neutral", but the projectile still has fast forward movement, thus the gyroscope want's to point in the direction of travel. As gravity takes over, and the projectile returns to earth, the gyroscopic forces continue to want to naturally point in the direction of travel.  This is visible in "High Angle" artillery missions that still land with the round pointed at the ground, despite being fired at an extremely high angle.  

I could definitely see the forces of air on the front playing much more of a part on a football, being far less mass, but the principles of ballistics I would think would remain the same aside the drag vs mass differences.  

Not a scientist, just a redleg that's curious.

Author: @davidmesiti6130
Content:
Awesome video, but I’m surprised there was no discussion at all about the laces. The laces certainly have an effect, if nothing more than exaggerating the natural movement of the ball. The laces do (at least) two things: 1) change the weight distribution/balance of the ball and 2) affect drag disproportionately on that side of the ball. Baseball pitchers use the laces on a baseball to take advantage of these physics and create pitches that move. Another example: If you look at a classic wiffle ball, the holes in it are not evenly distributed around the ball, they’re offset to one side of the equator, which allows those balls to be thrown with a huge amount of movement. 

Perhaps it’s true that a hypothetical “laceless” football would still fade to the throwing arm side based on the physics you described in the video, but I wonder how much the laces exaggerate this movement (or do something else to it). How do the laces contribute to wobble? So many questions about the laces. 

Also, @bee_lovin brought up sniper bullets and rifling… it just makes me wonder about a few things. How much spin-drift is happening? Is it 1 ft @ 1,000 yds or 10 ft/1,000 yds? I assume it’s parabolic…

Furthermore (and to tie it back to our football’s laces) I wonder about a hypothetical perfectly smooth bullet. I know that every single bullet fired has imperfections, however microscopic, which is related to why rifling helps. How does this apply to the football - perfectly smooth vs. with laces (and the grooves of the segments, which I haven’t even mentioned yet)?

Anyway, awesome video. Awesome that Tom was a part of it.

Author: @kennyrosenyc
Content: As a former football player (high school and college) I would say that this is NOT the biggest misconception in football. The biggest misconception is that (for some reason) offensive linemen are slow. An offensive lineman has to be able to block or 'catch'  a linebacker. A linebacker has to be able to tackle a wide receiver. Wide receivers are, generally, the fastest guys on the field. You have never had your life truly 'fact-checked' until you have been hit by a guy who is 6'5" tall, 300lbs. and who runs the 40-yard dash in 4.9 seconds. It's probably like getting hit by a dump truck at full speed. And a 4.9 second 40 is pedestrian. I ran the 40, for the first time, in high school at 300lbs. in 5.0 seconds. I've seen guys run way faster times at heavier weights. And it's because sprinting is a 'power' move, much more like jumping rope than jogging.

Author: @ExpatriotSilencers
Content: Derek, you should consider a second video looking at these principles as applied to bullets.  Bullets do the exact same thing as a football but the forces involved are much higher.  A rifle bullet will spin at 100,000 to 150,000 rpm.  Bullets also nose over at long range but it is possible to over stabilize a bullet by altering the rifling twist rate, which can result in the bullet staying nose up at the end of the parabolic curve.  Bullets also wander off to one side, which is known as spin drift.  At long range, bullets can also be affected by the rotation of the earth.  Its a pretty fascinating topic.

Content: It's a great video as always from Veritasium. However I find it weird that there is no analysis on how the spin speed will impact the pitch. In the video, it even measured that Brady's throw had a rotation of 628rpm, but there is no analysis of what an optimal rotation speed is. I would imagine that a high speed will give a high angular momentum to help keep the ball along its axis, but it will also cause less "wobbling" to cause turn over, and probably more side-way lift to sway the ball to the side. The fact that Brady only applies the spin through his wrist at the end of the pitch seems to suggest that the optimal rotation speed is not very high.

I won't be surprised if the reason the ball pitches down is similar to why seriously heavy, completely solid objects will rotate after being stopped. Author: @drk2592
Content: Physics professor here.  Nice update to the Drew Brees Sports Science video, which I've often used when explaining gyroscopes and torque-free precession.  Note that the discussion starting around 18:00 is bogus.  The viewer will think that the air flow causes the wobble.  Not true!  The wobble is exactly the phenomenon of torque-free precession, and will be there even in a vacuum.  The Sports Science video remarks on the  consistency of  the wobble to spin ratio,  erroneously attributing this to Drew Brees's consistency, but really the ratio is determined by the relative size of the two moments of inertia of the football.  The air flow is responsible for the turn-over, but not the wobble itself.

Author: @MikeyAntonakakis
Content:
Former punter here, who was maybe wayyy too cerebral/physics nerdy about it - I had a lot of time to play around with spirals. A “good” punt (at least in terms of distance, hangtime, and accuracy) spirals just like a nice throw - with some balance between imparting rotational vs linear energy that can be controlled by a decent punter; more spin is more stable but you lose some speed, and vice versa, so to maximize distance and hangtime there’s a Goldilocks balance between spin and linear speed. 

I didn’t go super far with punting (a little college football), but I did manage to get a lot of control over what the ball did (at least on a good day). I could make it turn over or not turn over at will, could control the bounce if desired (such as making it bounce straight towards the sideline in a “too far for field goal but too short for a big punt” situation). I never could quite wrap my head around WHY the ball would turn over even though I could control it, glad this video finally gave me the answer after a couple decades of head scratching!

Punting into the wind was always challenging - but eventually figured out that launching the ball at a low angle (say 20-30deg vs more normal 45ish) would create a weird trajectory - the ball would initially generate noticeable lift and actually curve upwards to a steeper trajectory, then as it lost some momentum would enter a more normal downward parabola shape. This minimized loss to distance with a headwind, since it got some good horizontal distance initially but still got sufficient height/hang time for the guys to get down field to cover it. If you just let it rip like normal, you could still get good hangtime but the distance would be terrible - there were more than a few instances where just for fun I put the ball on a steeper-than-normal trajectory (maybe 35ish yards with huge hangtime under normal conditions) during super windy practice days and had it land more or less behind me!

Author: @asdffdsa8863
Content:
Interestingly, much of the "engineering" was empirical rather than theoretical. Players naturally discovered that a tighter spiral flew better, and manufacturers gradually refined the shape based on this feedback. Modern computational fluid dynamics has since confirmed why these intuitive improvements worked, but the basic design was perfected through trial and error long before engineers could model airflow patterns around the ball.

The NFL's official ball specifications haven't changed significantly since 1934, suggesting the design reached an optimal balance relatively early in its evolution.

Author: @nikitavanhoose405
Content: I'm no expert, but I did get some training and instruction in highschool, in the state of Kentucky by Tim Couch. Tim played his highschool ball for the Leslie Co Eagles, where he became a 5 star QB. He would go on to have an all time great career for the Kentucky Wildcats in the SEC, and was drafted 1st overall to the Cleveland Browns, but the NFL didn't work out for him for numerous different reasons. I played QB a few counties North of Leslie Co, for the Lawrence Co Bulldogs. He he taught me a few things that, up to that point, no one else was teaching, and I haven't seen anyone teach since. Tom Brady is correct about having a loose grip on the football, but that is solely dependent on having big hands with long fingers that can wrap around the ball. If you have smaller hands, such as myself, then you want to keep the ball away from your palm and pad of your hand, with most of your grip on your fingertips, then you want to squeeze it hard with your fingertips. Tom is 6 ft- 4 inches, while I'm only 5ft - 11 inches. Tim Couch also corrected me on something he saw me doing that helped  my accuracy tremendously. He explained that way too often people, whether they realize they're doing it or not, people try to aim the point of the football at their target, and I was doing this as well. He taught me to keep my wrist loose and allow the football to turn sideways during my forward motion. He explained that if everything else is correct, and I have aimed at the target correctly, with proper mechanics and follow through, then the wind and the aerodynamics of the ball would straighten and correct itself. So basically, you want to retrain your brain to forget that the ball is oblong with points, and basically throw it like any other perfectly round ball. Once I realized that I was doing this and adjusted for it, that single thing improved my accuracy more than anything else I ever learned. I went on to have a pretty decent high School career at quarterback, especially for a 5 ft 11 kid with smaller hands. I actually got a full-ride scholarship for the Western Kentucky Hilltoppers, where I would help lead them to a 1-AA national championship as a starter in 2002. We beat McNeese State, 34-14. I've now had a long career as an NFL assistant coach, with numerous different NFL franchises. I'm not giving away my identity, order location of where I'm coaching now, but it's not very hard to find.

Author: @Battleborn357
Content: One thing I learned about throwing a football. How hand placement/grip on the football affects throwing depth, control, and spiraling when airborne. Tom has his middle finger off the laces, and his thumb and pointer finger wrapped toward the top cone part of the ball. This obviously is his style and what he is comfortable with. I always found it more comfortable to have my middle finger placed on the 1st lace. As I released the ball, my middle finger is what I mostly used to spin the ball. Naturally, because the middle finger is the strongest beside the thumb. This placement gripped my thumb and pointer almost perfectly to the white line of the ball. It gave me better control/grip and tighter spirals. It also allowed me to throw much deeper passes, even though I didn't have the strongest arm

Spin is the issue that the Mythbusters missed when doing their research on shooting a gun into the air.  They correctly figured out that a falling bullet will tumble (much like a football) but incorrectly assumed that the bullet would start it's downward trajectory by just falling.

A bullet fired from a gun spins, and unless fired (and travels to its apex) at a perfect 90° angle to the ground it will travel in an arc, which allows the bullet to keep spinning and to accelerate to a higher speed than a tumbling bullet on the way back down.

Author: @qdav5
Content:
The fact that a football (and a spinning projectile) with a right-hand spin will "drift" to the right was hard for me to comprehend when I started working with spinning projectiles as an engineer.  I grew up playing baseball, and I was a pitcher, so I knew that a baseball with a right-hand spin curved to the left.  This is a well-known consequence of the Magnus effect, and I assumed a spinning projectile would behave similarly.  Yes, the axis of a baseball with a right-hand spin points up (or at least upward), whereas a projectile's axis is nearly parallel to the ground, and that does make a big difference.  However, since gravity pulls a flying projectile towards the ground, the projectile nose points ever-so-slightly upward relative to the airflow around it, resulting in a small positive angle of attack.  Therefore, the Magnus effect comes into play and imposes a force that pushes the projectile to the left (aft-looking-forward).  
    BUT!  Since the projectile is spinning, the gyroscopic effect, reacting to the gravity-induced downward motion of the projectile, causes the nose of the projectile to point slightly to the right (assuming a right-hand spin).  This is called the "yaw of repose" and since the nose is pointed right , aerodynamic forces will push the projectile to the right.  
    So the angle of attack results in a Magnus effect that pushes the spinning projectile to the left and aerodynamic forces related to the yaw of repose push the projectile to the right.  It is almost always true that the angle of attack and the yaw of repose will both be small for a stable spinning projectile, and as a consequence, the "right-pushing" aerodynamic forces resulting from the yaw of repose will be larger than the "left-pushing" forces resulting from the Magnus effect.  That is why a spinning projectile, and a spinning football, with a right-hand spin will drift to the right.  

    < Edit >  Thank you for going to all the trouble of reading this.  I really just wanted to write it to prove to myself that I still remembered that particular aspect of the mechanics of spinning projectiles.

Content:
I saw a video last year about a punter whose kicks were difficult to catch. Video showed receivers lunging left and right at the last moment as they tried to catch the ball. Almost like a knuckleball.

My hunch is he's figured out a certain angle and spin rate of the football at which the Dzhanibekov effect kicks in with just the right period. If the period is too short, the ball wobbles too much and the trajectory changes of the wobbles average out. If the period is too long, the ball's wobble turns into a drift in just one direction. But wobble it between these two extremes and it'll change direction every few seconds, confusing receivers. Would be interesting to see a video on that.

Author: @mammy24
Content:
Taking a guess here, at 10:35 in the video. The spin wants to orient itself with the acceleration, meaning that just like the top the football will orient towards is accelerating it with the most force. The ball starts by accelerating in the hand of the QB, then as gravity takes over as the dominate acceleration force, it curves towards the ground. The constant rate of gravity means that the angle changes in step with the angle of the throw. The spin is what keeps the outside forces such as air resistance from imparting too much of a force and overcoming the angular momentum leaving only gravity and gyroscope of the spinning ball keeps it from skewing off due to wind resistance.

This would mean that in space, absent any apparent acceleration from outside bodies, the ball wouldn't change it's angle. It's not about the weight at the front, it's about the spin and acceleration.

Author: @Washington-Dreaming
Content: I think it can be argued that in his prime Aaron Rodgers might’ve been the best passer ever.  But if you take a field and make the length the X axis and a line orthogonal through the field the Z axis, and you throw straight ahead the initial speed of the ball in the x direction should be determined partially by the initial angle thrown.  So speed(X) = speed(total)  * cos(theta) where theta is the initial angle with respect to the Z axis.  So speed(X) is max when theta equals zero as cos(0) = 1.  But Aaron tended to throw flat passes because he had the arm strength to do it; you are fighting gravity and time in the Z direction obviously so you need the X speed to be high enough the ball won’t hit the ground before it reaches the receiver.  But this meant for Aaron the ball would travel the shortest distance possible reducing flight time. Integrate a parabola and its length is greater than a line segment with two same endpoints and Aaron could nearly approximate a line segment.  But of course he was really accurate too and his spiral was usually really tight so in-between arm strength, accuracy, spin and ball angle he probably nearly optimized what a human could do throwing a football.

Author: @silversage2205
Content:
Great video, but I think they don't explain this section about lift very well...or rather they're leaving something out on the way that makes it make more sense.

Assume a ball is thrown perfectly straight, with a tilt of 30 degrees up which perfectly matches the parabolic path of motion it will have.  There's no initial "tilt".  Would the ball still "turn over"?  
I assert the answer is yes.  Rephrasing that last statement, there's no deviation between the initial tilt of the ball and the line tangential to the curve of the parabola of its flight path.  However, as gyroscopic procession the only force causing the ball to turn over, the ball's tilt remains at 30 degrees to the ground while the parabola's tangential line instantly starts to "degrade".  One yard away from the passer, the ball would still have a tilt of 30 degrees but the parabola's tilt--it's tangential line--might be 29 degrees, for example. 
Now there is a net tilt to the ball so the force of drag due to wind is no longer evenly distributed.  The bottom of the ball is more exposed relative to the direction of  the force of air resistance--which is the inverse of the direction of travel--which would push the nose of the ball up.  If there is no rotation, this would mean the ball catches the wind a bit and lofts, slowing down.  If there is rotation, instead of pushing the nose of the ball up, this force pushes the nose of the ball in a direction 90 degrees along the rotation just as they explain in the video.  For a left-handed QB who throws with a counter-clockwise rotation as viewed from the back of the ball, the nose of the is pushed left.  For a right-handed QB the nose is pushed right.  This is the mechanic that powers the whole operation and which the video explains.  
What the video kind of leaves out is the change in the tilt of the ball relative to the tilt of the parabola over time.  Assuming the ball is caught at the same height it was released from, over the course of the flight the total change in tilt of the parabola's tangential line as measured to the ground will be double it's starting angle.  If it started at 30 above flat, it ends at 30 below flat, a total change of 60 degrees.  This deviation in tilt is "applied" to the ball as it progresses along the parabola, and it is an upward tilt to the nose of the ball relative to the angle of motion.  Think of it as a small constant push on the bottom front of the ball.  Again, without rotation, this would push the nose of the ball up.  But with rotation this pushes the nose of the ball to the right for right-handed QBs and to the left for left-handed QBs.  This is why the ball "spends more time wobbling to the right" for right-handed QBs.  That's not necessarily the most accurate phrase, though.  It would be more correct to say that this skews the tilt of the ball to the right relative to the flight path/the tangential line of the parabola.  This is why the ball has "lift" which pushes it to the side...right for righties left for lefties.
Also, that lift is proportional to the total change in angle which means it's proportional to the starting angle of the throw--it's actually proportional to gravity which determines the parabola but let's not get into that any further.  

In practice, that means it is more noticeable for lofted/touch and lob passes than bullet passes, and it also means its typically more noticeable for bigger throws, which tend to have steeper angles of release.

Author: @wittsullivan8130
Content: Any projectile that spins is going to have "windage" where the projectile acts like a paddlewheel and drifts towards the direction of the spin. Windage also means how much you correct for wind drift. Windage was also the term used in musketry for the gap between the projectile and the smooth bore. The British thought the gas pressure from the powder burning would leak out equally around the projectile, stabilizing the ball in the smoothbore so it would leave in the exact center of the muzzle.

This video is an example of how academics always get it wrong Even when they have good data. It is why America is not elevating and our understanding because they inherently believe researchers know what they're talking about.

It is the rotation of the threads that causes the drift. Also remember the threads themselves have extra drag.

Author: @error.418
Content: 23:09 In skydiving we clarify what we mean by the effective "wind" by adding the term "relative." In freefall, the local weather's wind going, say, parallel to the ground does move us and causes some drift, but the much more impactful "relative wind" is the perceived air movement along our direction of travel, our falling direction. Same for the football, sure it will be affected by what people think of when you say "wind," but what really affects it the most (up to a point, unless you're getting really nasty weather wind) is the "relative wind" which is along its direction of travel. So even in a dome with no ambient air movement, no "wind," throwing the ball through the air provides a "relative wind" which affects the ball. So when he says "it's because wind" he means "it's because air" and specifically that you're throwing an object through air.

Author: @bighomiedave24
Content: 3:14 In Australia where rugby league and rugby union is dominant (2 similar but very different games), we pass the ball across tbe line of scrimmage with the aim of passing backwards. Due to this, whilst we usually throw a spiral pass (most efficient pass and fastest speed), we also pass/throw the rugby ball flat (no spiral). Known as the "lofted/flat pass", the slower change of pace of the flat pass and the loftiness of travel, the way the air manipulates the travel path of the ball compared to a normal spiral pass, combined with the way the ball travels in the air pointing in a north/south direction instead of the traditional east/west direction a spiral pass causes makes the flat pass very useful and quite descriptive for running plays requiring players to run through tight defensive holes at opposing angles to the passer.

Author: @Ifishmo
Content: isn't all of this just normal ballistic physics?  The football veers to the right for a right handed thrown spiral due to the phenomena called 'spin drift', more specifically this is due to 'yaw of repose'.  Yaw of Repose is where the spin axis does not align with the arc axis (nose up) and this difference is where the pressure difference is applied to the bottom side of the nose which is where the gyroscopic progression effect is seen by slightly shifting spin axis to the right.  You can toss in a little magnus effect too but this will be very subtle (more affected by crosswinds but the little affect it will have will be due to how long the football drops) and in this case with a right handed throw (clockwise spin as viewed from the thrower) the magnus affect would slightly push the ball to the left.   Odd this was presented in this way, not the usual clear and concise explanations we're used to from this channel.  The football is nothing more than a goofy shaped bullet, long range ballistics have been well sorted out since before WWII.

Why isn’t gravity and aerodynamics a consideration for the footballs alignment through its parabolic arc? 

The spiral keeps the ball pointed in the direction that is less resistant to changes. It can’t stay pointed up because more air is pushing against a larger surface.

So as gravity changes the ball’s direction… the spiral keeps the ball pointed in the direction of travel. 

The spiral is the key. As the spiral slows the ball loses its ability to stay aligned. A slow spiral will keep the nose of the ball pointed up.

Author: @danielsondiecastracing
Content:
Those gyroscopic forces are also at play in Disc Golf. Disc manufacturers know about these forces and are able to design discs to take advantages of these forces to create discs that have different flight paths. While Tom Bradys flight path will always go a little to the right, a disc golf disc can "turn" to the right and then "fade" to the left at the end if you throw with a clockwise rotation (or the opposite with a counterclockwise rotation). This is referred to as the "S-Curve" flight path. Different discs use lift, drag, and gyroscopic precession to alter the amount of "turn' and "fade" a disc has to create the shot you are looking for. 

When you see disc golfers out on the course, they may be bagging 20-30 different discs designed to create different shot shapes at different distances. You should 100% look into that for your followup video. It's super cool and it's why disc golf has been my new favorite sport for a few years now.

Author: @rangacharivijay
Content: Hi Veritasium et al - I am a huge fan of you guys, and this is one more gem you have created.  But I want to point out one critical omission in your analysis - the effect of LACES (stitches on the ball).  The wobble and precession will be way different if the ball did not have the laces. In some sense, a laceless ball will be an "ideal" football where it can experience a symmetrical spin. Yet we know from spin physics that the gravitational force can also affect precession around the angular momentum vector.  This effect in a real football case is augmented because of the lace.  The airflow is dramatically disrupted by the lace, which forces the air flow to be non-laminar and anisotropic, making it wobble. However, a spin around the ball's long axis will make this effect more isotropic, so it moves without a wobble.  Just wanted to point out this fact. Besides this, as I said, it is a fantastic work, and I was doubly excited to see Tom Brady!!!   Keep it going, guys.

Author: @zacharyjeffares8158
Content:
Sports Science did this with Drew Brees, and due to the way a football is shaped, the perfect spiral is actually one with a very small “wobble”, where the nose draws a very small circle in front of the ball. However if the circle gets too small the ball will become unstable and try to flip over.
The tailing to one side is a product of which way the ball is spinning. This effect is more weird in baseball as when those are thrown, they are thrown with backspin most of the time, not sidespin- and will still tail to the “arm side” simply from how the ball is released. One side has more drag than the other- the Magnus Effect.
The last thing is the angle of release. Most objects require at least a very small upward trajectory in order to get distance, with the exception of discs and ping pong balls. What’s interesting about footballs is that they require a higher angle (pointing the nose up) than almost any other thrown object to go really far.

Content: Interesting fact about rifling you didn't mention. It was developed before we discovered spin stabilization, and thus wasn't originally developed to improve accuracy. Originally it was developed because black powder (the predecessor of gunpowder) burns very dirty and leaves lots of residue in the barrel, which because they were using muzzleloaders then made the gun harder to load with every shot. The rifling was meant to give the fouling and debris a place to accumulate without casuing issues loading. It was spiraled in the belief that straight grooves would let more gas escape around the bullet. Pretty soon after it became common people noticed their rifles were more accurate

I think that all objects fly because they collect the drag in concentrated such locations. They steer by manipulating drag. 

An object thrown collects the energy on the heavy &/or front side, the drag on the lite &/or rear side. 

Spinning objects spin because of reduced dominance of the energy bearing area by weight distribution similarities, &/or drag distribution similarities. 

The variations are not enough to produce an absolute state of dominance or indominance between energy & drag. Such as an egg shape or football. 

It is movement in the organization of energy & drag that produces more such movements in the constant search for dominance. 

Because of the high tolerance or low differential between energy & drag, the motion from one state to another produces overlapping effects  expressed in constant motion.thus the spin. 

The football is a highly specialized case (double, if you will); between the front & the back horizontally, & infinitesimal in the vertical.

Content: I can think of one thing that slipped by you, but all the components are actually in your video. Projectile drift. Applicable to rifles, artillery and more, it's one of the fundamental considerations of long distance shots and ballistic solutions from ground based artillery, to aerial gun platforms. As a projectile fires from a barrel with a right hand twist (clockwise when viewing from rear of projectile) it applies a force on the air below it (more drag) and as Newton put it, for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The air below it pushes back. That same gyroscopic precession mentioned before applies this force 90 degrees into rotation (from the left side) causing the projectile to drift to the right. Likewise to the wobble, this drift causes another force from the air it drifts into, which manifests into the bottom of the projectile, causing a projectile to resist some of the pull of gravity and actually rise momentarily,  called "projectile jump".

Author: @Pol-Torres-Campos
Content: I think this can be simplified as follows: The center of pressure is located toward the back, which influences the rotational momentum and pitch angle of the ball. The wobbling motion results from aerodynamics dynamic forces acting on the ball and its angular momentum during its ascent and descent. Instability increases due to the cumulative effects of aerodynamic losses. Additionally, the induced angular momentum is not perfectly aligned with the ball’s geometric axis, which further contributes to the unsteady motion. The left and right deviation can be explained by the Magnus effect — in this case, air moving along the Z-axis (perpendicular to the direction of motion) interacts with the ball’s rotation, causing lateral deviation.

Author: @anteshell
Content:
25:37 I think this sequence is entirely wrong. Being intuitively able to exploit physical phenomenon to your advantage is neither scientific nor requires you to understand the phenomenon at all.

Let's say I draw with a pen. I know that the colour is initially in the pen but as I pull the tip along the paper  the colour transfers to it. Depending on how I handle the pend and make the lines, the colour will transfer in different intensities and form dimensionally different line. All of that is intuitive, even if I knew very little about the vast amount of different physical interactions that different pens have to hold the colour, transfer it to the tip and finally from the tip to the paper. Understanding the results of an action is entirely different than understanding why exactly that action produces those results from physics standpoint.

Even easier example. Everybody from the age of 3 should know that if you hold and item and let go of it, it will drop down. However, not many people at that age understands what gravity is and how it works. 

So, no. Tom Brady is not a modern day Isaac Newton and is not scientific at all. Understands the results from his actions to the point that he's become one of the most skilled people in exploiting them, but in the end does not understand exactly why things happens as they do. Just that they happen.

Content: In cricket (the sport), the ball "swings" after release, and the extent and nature of swing is based on a number of factors. Author: @XtomJamesExtra
Content: You guys missed a major component, and it's Magnus effect and the laces/grip point. In the initial part of the throw as it travels upward, the procession helps to stabilize the ball along the trajectory until it reaches its apogee and the ball levels out. The ball as it rotates is generating lift due to Magnus effect, and this effect is equally balanced all the way until the apogee of travel. However, as the ball begins its descent, the grip disrupts the leading lift generated by the tip and front end of the ball by disrupting the boundary layer that's created due to the spin. Thus the only segment of the ball that is generating lift is the trailing end. This causes the ball to tip forward and to align with the trajectory arc.  In effect, there's far more complex physics happening with a football than what seems apparent.

Author: @sierraecho21031
Content: As a student pilot currently flying the PA-28, this video is fascinating and I totally didn’t expect football to have so much relevance to aviation! One of the biggest misconceptions that students (and instructors!) often have is that precession is one of the "left-turning tendencies" that affect a single-engine aircraft. The three left-turning tendencies are torque, propellor slipstream, and p-factor, which I won’t go into here, but they all cause a yaw or roll to the left on takeoff in a modern single-engine aircraft with a propellor that turns clockwise (from the pilot’s perspective). However, gyroscopic precession actually works in the opposite direction, since a pitch up applies an outward force to the bottom of the prop and an inward force to the top, which is then shifted to an inward force to the right as precession acts 90° ahead of the direction of rotation. I feel like I never fully understood why precession is 90° ahead until I saw that great demonstration!
